open_obligations: Note that the judge is an LLM fine-tuned on human judgements, not a human judge.
Check whether the debaters actually produced refutations in the second turn.
Check confidence intervals on the 2-point debate versus double-consultancy gap.
in.other_title: Judge accuracy: debate 77%, double consultancy 75%, ensembled 72%, single consultancy 68%
in.rationale: Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that reference the other side. Arnesen et al. report debate 77% versus double consultancy 75% (both sides shown, no refutation) and that one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn ones, concluding either debaters fail to refute meaningfully or the judge does not benefit; the judge is an LLM, not a human.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether refutation between sides adds value over independent arguments, for trained Llama3-8B debaters and a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo judge on QuALITY-HARD

open_obligations: Note that Michael et al. compare debate with consultancy, not with a no-argument or single-turn condition.
Note that hiding the passage changes what the arguments must supply.
Check which design change (turns, interaction, hidden passage, debater skill) drives the difference.

Check whether Michael et al.'s debaters' counterarguments explicitly reference deficiencies in the other argument, as Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on; the cited passage says only that debaters are expected to defend their position against criticism.
in.other_title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert judges: 84% vs 74% on hard reading comprehension questions
in.rationale: Parrish et al. ask whether a multi-turn setting with explicit counterarguments is needed for debate to help. Michael et al. contrast their setting with the one- and two-turn debates of Parrish et al., in which debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy: their debates are unbounded in length, and debaters are expected to defend their position against criticism by their opponent for as long as the judge is not convinced of the answer. They report 84% judge accuracy for debate versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions; their judges have not read the source passage and see only expert arguments and short quotes selectively revealed by the debaters, and debaters are expert humans, so several factors differ.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether unbounded multi-turn debate helps human judges on hard reading comprehension questions

open_obligations: Note that two turns is still far from unbounded interactive debate.
Check that the follow-up's judges and time limits are comparable to those of the original study.
Check whether judges could read enough of the passage to bypass the arguments.
Check that the follow-up uses 2-option QuALITY questions with human-written arguments, since the cited passages do not say so.
in.other_title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments did not help humans on the authors' reading comprehension task
in.rationale: Parrish et al. (single-turn) ask whether a multi-turn setting with counterarguments is needed. The two-turn follow-up adds a second round of counter-arguments and reports that humans perform similarly regardless of whether they have access to arguments.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether adding explicit counter-arguments makes debate helpful to human judges, on the two-turn follow-up's reading comprehension task

text: The authors suggest that the arguments may have been more misleading than helpful to some workers because correct and incorrect arguments were independent of each other, whereas debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that explicitly reference deficiencies in the other argument. They pose whether a multi-turn setting is needed for debate to be helpful as a question for future research.
title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
